newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Mass. lawmakers scramble for budget accord.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mass. lawmakers scramble for budget accord.

text.p: Top state officials have their fingers crossed during this last full week before the fiscal 1998 year dawns in Massachusetts.

They are hoping that the half-dozen House and Senate conferees charged with crafting the final version of the new state budget will have worked through all their differences by mid-week so the $18.3 billion spending plan can be advanced to Gov. William Weld's desk.

House and Senate conferees have reportedly been working steadily for the past several weeks on particulars in the fiscal 1998 state budget. They were scheduled to work into the weekend in hopes of readying a final bill for action before the full House and Senate this week.

In addition to the differences between the branches over dollar amounts and language in individual budget line items, the conferees are also trying to negotiate major initiatives called for in the Senate's budget.

The Senate budget called for a series of tax cuts directed toward lower and middle-income Bay Staters, and for the abolition of county government. Since the Senate attached those measures to its budget, the House has acted on separate legislation endorsing its own version of the Senate's call for an increase in the per-child deduction parents can claim on their state income tax forms.
That action came last week when House Speaker Thomas Finneran told his House colleagues that state coffers continue to overflow and a tax cut is warranted.

The House also passed its own bill to have the state take over the crippled governance of Middlesex County. The House also called for a task force to analyze the liability of the remaining counties and report back early next year about how best to achieve a takeover.
House and Senate negotiators are also struggling to use an expected $400 million surplus that will be reflected on the books when the fiscal 1997 bookkeeping year ends on June 30.
Meanwhile, the State Administration Committee has scheduled two executive sessions this week to act on bills still pending including a plan to finance a $700 million convention center for Boston.
It was unclear as this week's session begins whether its members would seek an extension on, or vote to send on the measures to the House's new Long-Term Debt and Capital Expenditure Committee.

That panel has been conducting hearings and preparing a report on the state's extended debt obligations. If the proposed projects for Boston, Worcester, Springfield, Fall River and Western Massachusetts clear that committee, they will move on to the House Ways and Means Committee.
House Speaker Finneran, who had stalled progress on previous convention center proposals he believed saddled taxpayers with too much of its cost, now appears to be a believer in the project.

He has said the convention center bill will likely clear the House before this summer's recess. Finneran's support comes in the wake of an increased commitment from Boston's city government and Gov. Weld's willingness to raise the hotel tax in Boston and Cambridge if voters there agree to such an increase.
